newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Agriculture slowdown stunts Cambodia growth -ADB.
newsitem.headline: Agriculture slowdown stunts Cambodia growth -ADB.

text.p: Adverse weather helped slow growth in Cambodia's agriculture-based economy last year, with gross domestic product (GDP) growth slipping to 6.0 percent from 7.5 percent in 1995, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) said.

"In 1996, economic performance was constrained by the slowdown in agriculture, as once again crops suffered damage from heavy floods," the bank said in its Asian Development Outlook released on Thursday.

Floods along the Mekong River at the end of the May-November rainy season left hundreds of thousands of people homeless, killed more than 20 people and destroyed large areas of cropland. Environmentalists link the flooding to deforestation.
The agriculture sector grew only 1.5 percent against a hefty 6.5 percent a year earlier, while crops -- accounting for more than half of total agricultural output, grew by just 1.0 percent.
However, the country's small industrial sector grew 13.5 percent against 9.8 percent in 1995, with construction up 14 percent and textiles also showing a notable increase.

"The services sector, which accounts for 37 percent of GDP, expanded by 7.7 percent, slightly down from the previous year, and with the industry sector helped cushion the effects of agriculture's poor performance," the ADB report said.
It said consumer price increases, particularly food prices, accelerated in the latter part of the year as a result of the shortfall in agricultural supply.
The inflation rate stood at 10 percent against 3.5 percent a year earlier, but was expected to slow down to 5.0 percent in 1997 with the continuation of restrictive monetary policies.
Revenue receipts were below expectations, although as a result of expenditure restraint the overall fiscal deficit remained within targets at 609 billion riels ($225.6 million) or 7.4 percent of GDP.

The report said the current account deficit remained high and the country still relied heavily on external assistance to close the resource gap but reforms were expected to improve the budgetary situation through better tax administration and expenditure control.
Domestic exports increased in 1996 but total exports ($615 million) fell by 28.1 percent as a result of the substantial decline in re-exports. Total imports totalled $1.01 billion, down 14.1 percent.
The current account deficit, excluding official transfers, stood at $430 million or 14.1 percent of gross national product.

"Cambodia's debt in convertible currency at end-1996 was estimated to be $642 million or 22 percent of GNP. Official public and publicly guaranteed loans formed the bulk of this," the ADB report said.
It urged reform of the fiscal system and financial sector and said measures that promoted the expansion of private sector investment should be pursued vigorously.

It recommended allocating more resources to social services such as health and education to improve living standards and said increasing the pace of rural development was "crucial to achieving the goals of food supply stability and poverty alleviation".
